clinical_knowledge.topic: Simple Finger Laceration evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Simple Finger Laceration is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Simple Finger Laceration, ruling out tendon or digital nerve injury, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Simple Finger Laceration.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Flexor tendon laceration without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inability to bend the fingertip or reduced sensation — suggests tendon or nerve injury needing specialist referral.
management_principles: Evaluate distal sensation (two-point discrimination) and tendon function (flexor digitorum superficialis/profundus) to rule out tendon or digital nerve injury
Irrigate wound, administer local lidocaine, and suture
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A clean cut to the finger requiring assessment of tendon function and nerve sensation before simple wound closure — the exam, not the wound's appearance alone, rules out deeper structural injury.
red_flags: Inability to bend the fingertip or reduced sensation — suggests tendon or nerve injury needing specialist referral

must_ask.say: How did you cut it, and how long ago?
Is the bleeding controlled with pressure?
Can you feel normal touch on your fingertip?
Can you bend and straighten your finger normally?
When was your last tetanus shot?

history.answer: I cut my left index finger with a kitchen knife while chopping vegetables about an hour ago, and I need someone to look at it.
I was slicing carrots for dinner with a kitchen knife, and the blade slipped and sliced into the palm side of my left index finger.
It happened about an hour ago, right around 6 PM.
It is on the palm side of my left index finger, across the middle part, and looks about two centimeters long.
The knife was clean and the vegetables were washed. There was no dirt, rust, or broken glass, and it definitely was not an animal or human bite.
No, the knife blade was intact. I do not feel anything stuck inside the cut.
It bled quite a bit onto the cutting board, but it was not spurting or pulsing. I held a clean kitchen towel firmly against it, and the bleeding stopped.
No, I do not have any numbness or tingling in the fingertip, and the touch feels normal compared to my other fingers.
I can bend and straighten the tip and all the joints of my finger normally, though moving it stings a bit right at the cut.
It has a sharp stinging throb right at the cut, maybe a 4 or 5 out of 10, but the rest of my finger feels fine.
No, there is no redness spreading out, no pus, and no bad smell, and I have not had any fever or chills.
No, nothing like that at all. It was completely an accident while I was preparing dinner.
I was worried whether I might have cut a tendon or nerve, and I wondered if I might need stitches.
I am really nervous about the pain of getting stitches because needles and suturing scare me.
I would like the cut cleaned properly, checked to make sure nothing is damaged, and stitched up if it needs it.
I had a tetanus booster shot about eight years ago after a minor scrape, but nothing since then.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or bleeding disorders.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never stayed in a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, aspirin, blood thinners, or over-the-counter pain relievers.
No, I do not take steroids, and I do not have any conditions that weaken my immune system.
I do not have any drug allergies, including to antibiotics or local numbing shots.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine once or twice a month, and I had not been drinking today.
I work as a graphic designer, so having full use of my hands is essential for my job. I live with my husband in an apartment.
There is no family history of bleeding disorders or severe chronic diseases. My parents are both healthy.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my cycles are regular every 28 days.
There is no possibility of pregnancy. My husband and I use barrier contraception consistently.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 74 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable young female sitting up and applying firm direct pressure with a clean cloth over her left index finger, in no acute distress.

A 2 cm clean, linear laceration across the palmar aspect of the left index finger over the middle phalanx, with no devitalized tissue, active bleeding, visible foreign body, or exposed tendon or bone.
Full active flexion against resistance at both the distal interphalangeal joint (FDP) and proximal interphalangeal joint (FDS), with intact extension across all digits.
Two-point discrimination is 4 mm along both the radial and ulnar digital nerve distributions of the index finger distal to the laceration, with symmetric light touch sensation.
Brisk capillary refill under 2 seconds at the left index fingertip, with strong and symmetric radial pulses bilaterally.
Full active and passive range of motion of the left wrist, hand, and fingers without deformity or joint effusion, with mild localized discomfort at the wound on full finger extension.
